title: Globalization, Localization, and Culture Concepts
description: Understand the core concepts behind ASP.NET Core globalization and localization: cultures, UICulture, and how .NET handles culture-specific formatting.

terms.definition: Designing and building an application so it can support many cultures and regions without code changes. Includes date, number, and currency formatting.
Adapting a globalized application for a specific locale by providing translated strings and culturally appropriate content.
The umbrella term covering both globalization and localization — making software usable worldwide.
A .NET object (System.Globalization.CultureInfo) that defines formatting rules for dates, numbers, currencies, and sort order for a specific language/region combination like 'en-US' or 'fr-FR'.
A separate .NET setting that controls which resource file (translated strings) is loaded. Usually matches Culture but can differ.
The .NET class that represents a culture. Examples: new CultureInfo('en-US'), new CultureInfo('ja-JP').

data.text: These two terms are often used together, but they mean different things. Understanding the distinction is important before you write any code:

cards.title: Globalization (G11n)
cards.description: The process of building your app so it CAN support many cultures.

cards.title: Localization (L10n)
cards.description: The process of providing actual translations and culture-specific content for each supported locale.
pros: Makes your app usable for real users worldwide
cons: Needs a process for keeping translations in sync

data.title: Think of it like a house
data.text: Globalization is building a house with multi-voltage wiring and standard-sized pipes so it works anywhere. Localization is painting the walls, choosing furniture, and translating the welcome mat for each country.
.NET uses standard culture codes in the format `language-REGION`. The first part is a two-letter ISO language code; the optional second part is a two-letter ISO country/region code:
The `CultureInfo` class is how .NET represents a culture. You create it with a culture code string and it provides all the formatting rules automatically:

data.title: C# — creating and using CultureInfo objects
data.content: CultureInfo objects provide formatting methods that automatically adapt to each culture's conventions.

data.text: ASP.NET Core tracks two separate culture values per request. This separation gives you fine-grained control over what users see:

rows: Which resource file is loaded for strings
en-US / fr-FR = English dates, French text

data.title: Why would Culture and UICulture differ?
data.text: In Canada, a user might want English formatting (dates, currency) but French text. In that case: Culture = en-CA, UICulture = fr-CA. This level of control is available but most sites set them to the same value.
When a culture is set, .NET uses it automatically for all culture-sensitive operations. You don't need to pass the culture to every method call — it's stored in thread-level context:

data.title: C# — culture is applied automatically
data.content: Once CultureInfo.CurrentCulture is set, all ToString(), parsing, and formatting calls use it automatically.

data.caption: How a culture code flows through an ASP.NET Core request
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[Browser sends request] --> B{Where does culture come from?}
    B -->|Query string| C[?culture=fr-FR]
    B -->|Cookie| D[.AspNetCore.Culture]
    B -->|Browser header| E[Accept-Language: fr]
    B -->|URL segment| F[/fr/Home/Index]
    C --> G[Localization Middleware]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Set CurrentCulture = fr-FR]
    G --> I[Set CurrentUICulture = fr-FR]
    H --> J[Controller/View runs]
    I --> J
    J --> K[Dates, numbers formatted in French]
    J --> L[Resource file fr.resx loaded for strings]

data.title: Neutral vs Specific cultures
data.text: Neutral cultures (e.g., 'fr') represent a language without a region. Specific cultures (e.g., 'fr-FR') include a region. Always use specific cultures for formatting and as defaults. Use neutral cultures only as fallbacks.

data.title: Exercise: Format the Same Value in 5 Cultures
data.description: Write a small C# program that demonstrates how one date and one number look in five different cultures.
steps: Create a new console app: dotnet new console -n CultureDemo.
In Program.cs, create five CultureInfo objects: en-US, en-GB, fr-FR, es-ES, and ja-JP.
Display the long date, short date, currency, and number format for each culture for the same DateTime and decimal values.
Observe how the decimal separator, date order, and currency symbol change.
Add a neutral culture like 'fr' and note what happens when you call ToString() on it — it falls back to the specific culture.
data.expectedOutcome: A console output clearly showing how the same values look different across cultures, reinforcing why globalization starts with CultureInfo.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Globalization (G11n) is building your app to support many cultures. Localization (L10n) is providing the actual translations.
Culture codes use the format 'language-REGION': en-US, fr-FR, es-ES.
Culture controls date/number/currency formatting; UICulture controls which resource file loads.
CultureInfo objects are created with a culture code string and provide all formatting rules automatically.
Once a culture is set, .NET applies it everywhere — no manual ToString(culture) calls needed.
data.takeaway: Mastering culture concepts is the foundation for everything else in this module. Once you understand CultureInfo, the rest of the implementation follows naturally.

items.question: Do I need a culture code for every country?
items.answer: No. Start with the languages your users speak. A single 'fr' culture covers all French speakers, while 'fr-FR' and 'fr-CA' let you differentiate France from Canada.

items.question: What happens if I request a culture that isn't registered?
items.answer: ASP.NET Core falls back to the DefaultRequestCulture you configured. No exception is thrown — the app just uses the fallback culture.

items.question: Can I change culture at runtime per user?
items.answer: Yes. The localization middleware sets culture per-request. Each request can have a different culture based on the provider's result.

items.question: Is there a performance cost to setting culture?
items.answer: Minimal. CultureInfo objects are cached. The localization middleware adds a small amount of overhead per request, which is negligible for most applications.
